# Multimodal Models: Fusion and Generation {#sec-multimodal}

@sec-diffusion gave the generative engine for pixels and @sec-beyond-text argues
about where multimodality is heading; this chapter is the stack in between. It
covers how vision is fused into a language model so the model can understand an
image, and how the diffusion engine is wired into a system that generates images
and video. By the end a reader can explain the two ways to bolt vision onto a
language model, the two routes to text-to-image, why video generation needs a
latent autoencoder, and the live split between unified and modular multimodal
models.

## Fusing vision into language

The shared space comes first. CLIP contrastively aligns an image encoder and a
text encoder over 400 million pairs into a single embedding space, so an image
can be classified zero-shot by matching it against text prompts
[@radford2021clip], and that aligned space is the conditioning signal much of
image generation later reuses. To make a language model itself see, two fusion
patterns compete. Cross-attention injection keeps both towers frozen and inserts
trainable layers between them: Flamingo bridges a frozen vision encoder and a
frozen language model with gated cross-attention blocks trained on interleaved
image-text, enabling few-shot multimodal tasks [@alayrac2022flamingo].
Projection instead meets the modalities at the input: LLaVA projects a vision
encoder's features into the language model's token space and fine-tunes on
GPT-4-generated visual instruction data [@liu2023llava]. The design axis is how
much of each tower stays frozen and where the modalities meet, deep inside via
cross-attention or shallow at the input via a thin projection.

## Generating images

Built on the diffusion engine of @sec-diffusion, two system routes reach
text-to-image. The diffusion route conditions a diffusion model on text. Imagen
uses a large frozen text encoder with cascaded diffusion and reports that scaling
the text encoder helps sample fidelity and alignment more than scaling the
diffusion model itself [@saharia2022imagen]. DALL-E 2 splits the problem: a prior
maps the caption to a CLIP image embedding, and a diffusion decoder renders an
image from that embedding [@ramesh2022dalle2]. Latent diffusion, the Stable
Diffusion line of @sec-diffusion, is the open variant. The autoregressive route
is the diffusion-versus-tokens tension of @sec-nar-lm applied to pixels: tokenize
the image into a learned discrete codebook with VQGAN [@esser2021vqgan], then
model those tokens with a transformer, which Parti scales to twenty billion
parameters as text-to-image sequence-to-sequence over image tokens
[@yu2022parti].

## Generating video

Video adds time, and time adds cost. The first step extended image diffusion with
a space-time factorized 3D U-Net to keep frames temporally coherent
[@ho2022videodiffusion]. The 2024 shift applies the diffusion transformer of
@sec-diffusion to spacetime latent patches, trained across variable durations,
resolutions, and aspect ratios; OpenAI's Sora is the prominent example, described
in a non-peer-reviewed report [@brooks2024sora]. What makes any of this tractable
is compression: a learned autoencoder shrinks pixels into a far smaller grid of
latent tokens before the quadratic-cost transformer runs over them.

:::: {.runnable}
```python
# Why video generation needs a latent autoencoder: count the tokens a diffusion
# transformer must attend over, in pixel space vs a compressed latent space.
fps, seconds = 24, 5
H = W = 512
patch = 2                          # transformer patch size in the working space
for name, f in [("pixel space", 1), ("latent (x8 VAE)", 8), ("latent (x16 VAE)", 16)]:
    h, w = H // f, W // f
    tokens = fps * seconds * (h // patch) * (w // patch)
    print(f"{name:18s} -> {tokens:>10,d} spacetime tokens")
print("attention is quadratic in tokens; latent compression is what makes video tractable")
```
::::

::: {.callout-important}
## What's contested
Whether one model should both understand and generate every modality, or whether
specialization wins, is unsettled. The unified bet trains a single any-to-any
model: Chameleon quantizes images to discrete tokens and trains one transformer
over interleaved image-text tokens, pure next-token prediction across modalities
[@chameleon2024], while Transfusion keeps images continuous and trains one
transformer with a next-token loss on text and a diffusion loss on images,
reporting that this beats quantizing everything [@zhou2024transfusion]. The
modular bet keeps a strong vision-language model for understanding and separate
specialized generators for images and video. The unified models are simpler to
compose and share representation across tasks; the modular ones let each piece be
the best of its kind and evolve independently. Which way it settles is open.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Constraint arrow
The visual tokenizer's compression ratio reaches back into what the generator can
afford. Attention is quadratic in token count, and a minute of video is millions
of pixels per frame, so generation is only tractable because a learned
autoencoder compresses pixels into a far smaller latent grid before the diffusion
transformer runs, the same latent move @sec-diffusion made for images and the
same token-count pressure @sec-serving-multimodal feels at serving time. The
generator's compute budget dictates how aggressive the visual tokenizer must be.
:::
